hints: Focus on how many moles of HCl were actually used, start with moles = concentration x volume in dm3.
Write the equation for calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid and notice that 1 mole of carbonate needs 2 moles of acid.
Convert your moles of carbonate into grams using Mr = 100.1, then express that as a percentage of the 2.00 g rock.
walkthrough:
**Find moles of HCl neutralised**

Only the calcium carbonate reacts, so all the acid tells us about carbonate. Convert volume to dm3 first.

$$\text{moles HCl} = c \times V = 0.500 \times \frac{36.0}{1000} = 0.0180 \, \text{mol}$$

**Use the 1 to 2 reacting ratio**

The balanced equation shows why we cannot use a 1 to 1 ratio:
$$\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So moles of carbonate are half the moles of acid.
$$\text{moles CaCO}_3 = \frac{0.0180}{2} = 0.00900 \, \text{mol}$$

**Convert to mass then to percentage**

Mr of $\text{CaCO}_3 = 40.1 + 12.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 100.1$.
$$\text{mass CaCO}_3 = 0.00900 \times 100.1 = 0.901 \, \text{g}$$
$$\% \, \text{CaCO}_3 = \frac{0.901}{2.00} \times 100 = 45.0\%$$

options.A: 22.5% is exactly half the correct value. It comes from halving twice, for example thinking 1 mole of CaCO3 needs 4 moles of HCl, so moles CaCO3 = 0.0180 / 4. The equation clearly needs only 2 HCl.
options.B: 45.0% is correct. 0.0180 mol HCl neutralises 0.00900 mol CaCO3, which has mass 0.901 g. In a 2.00 g sample this is 45.0% by mass.
options.C: 72.0% is too high and comes from an arithmetic or Mr slip. A mass of 1.44 g would be needed for 72%, which would require about 0.0144 mol CaCO3, not the 0.00900 mol given by the 1 to 2 ratio.
options.D: 90.1% is double the correct value. It is the classic trap of assuming a 1 to 1 ratio, so moles CaCO3 = moles HCl = 0.0180 mol, giving mass about 1.80 g. Always check the balanced equation: CaCO3 + 2HCl.
